course.title: Physics 101 (demo): Motion & Forces
course.overview_md:
**This is a sample course** written to show how FinalForge works; its "past papers" are sample questions, not real exams.

The course tells one story: first we learn to **describe** motion (displacement → velocity → acceleration → the SUVAT toolkit → projectiles), then we learn what **causes** changes in motion (Newton's second law, free-body diagrams, friction on slopes).

The sample final has 3 recurring question types: a **horizontal projectile** (≈ 10 marks), a **block on a rough slope** (≈ 10 marks) and a **uniform braking** problem (≈ 5 marks).

topics.name: Describing motion (kinematics)
topics.summary: Where things are, how fast, and how that changes.

concepts.name: Displacement & velocity
concepts.one_liner: Velocity is how fast your position changes, and in which direction.

detail.why_exists_md: Saying "I walked 5 km" doesn't tell anyone where you ended up. To predict *where* something will be, we need distance **with direction** (displacement) and speed **with direction** (velocity).
detail.what_it_does_md:
Lets you describe exactly where an object goes and how quickly its position changes.

**In one sentence:** velocity = how much your position changes each second, including which way.
detail.how_it_works_md:
1. Pick a starting point and a positive direction.
2. Displacement $s$ = final position − starting position (can be negative).
3. Velocity = displacement ÷ time: $v = s/t$ for steady motion.
detail.everyday_analogy_md: Walking to the school gate and back: you walked 400 m (distance) but your displacement is 0, because you're back where you started. Your *average velocity* over the round trip is 0 even though your legs are tired.
detail.visualize_md: Draw a number line. An arrow from start to finish is the displacement. The arrow's length per second is the velocity.

atomic_steps.everyday_link: how far the gate is from the door

atomic_steps.step_md: Divide by time taken = average velocity.

formulas.name: Average velocity
formulas.when_to_use_md: Steady motion, or for the *average* velocity. Not for changing speeds at an instant.

patterns_to_spot.signals_md: Give a sign or a direction with your answer.

common_traps.fix_md: Ask: does the direction matter here? If yes → displacement.

tips_tricks.tip_md: Always state your positive direction at the top of your working.

detail.mini_example_md: A runner goes 300 m east in 60 s then 100 m west in 40 s. Displacement $= 300 - 100 = 200$ m east; average velocity $= 200/100 = 2$ m/s east.
self_check: What's the difference between distance and displacement?
Can velocity be negative? What does that mean?

concepts.name: Acceleration
concepts.one_liner: Acceleration is how fast your velocity changes each second.

detail.why_exists_md: Things don't just move at one speed: cars speed up, balls slow down. We need a number for **how quickly velocity changes**, or we can't predict anything that speeds up or slows down.
detail.what_it_does_md:
Tells you how many m/s of velocity are added (or removed) every second.

**In one sentence:** acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time taken.
detail.how_it_works_md: If velocity goes from $u$ to $v$ in time $t$, the change is $v-u$; spreading it evenly over $t$ seconds gives $a = (v-u)/t$. Negative $a$ means velocity is decreasing in the positive direction (slowing down if you're moving forwards).
detail.everyday_analogy_md: Pocket money: if your savings go from \$10 to \$40 in 3 weeks, they grow by \$10 *per week*. Acceleration is the same thing for velocity: how many m/s you gain *per second*.
detail.visualize_md: Picture a speedometer needle. Acceleration is how fast the needle moves, not where it points.

atomic_steps.step_md: Keep the sign: negative = slowing (if moving +).

formulas.name: Acceleration
formulas.when_to_use_md: Constant acceleration, or the average acceleration over an interval.

patterns_to_spot.signals_md: Negative acceleration in the direction of motion.

common_traps.trap_md: Thinking zero velocity means zero acceleration.
common_traps.fix_md: A ball at the top of its throw has $v = 0$ but $a = g$ downwards.

common_traps.trap_md: Dropping the minus sign for deceleration.
common_traps.fix_md: Write $a$ with its sign; say "deceleration of 6.25 m/s²" only in words.

tips_tricks.tip_md: Units check: m/s divided by s = m/s².

detail.mini_example_md: A car goes from 10 m/s to 25 m/s in 5 s: $a = (25-10)/5 = 3\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.
self_check: Can something have zero velocity and non-zero acceleration?
What does a negative acceleration mean?

concepts.name: Constant-acceleration equations (SUVAT)
concepts.one_liner: Five linked quantities (s, u, v, a, t): know three, find the other two.

detail.why_exists_md: Exam questions give you a few facts about a motion and ask for something else. Without a toolkit linking them, you'd have to reason from scratch every time.
detail.what_it_does_md:
Four equations that connect displacement $s$, initial velocity $u$, final velocity $v$, acceleration $a$ and time $t$, valid whenever $a$ is constant.

**In one sentence:** list what you know, pick the equation that's missing the one you don't care about.
detail.how_it_works_md: Each equation leaves out exactly one of the five quantities. Write down the three you know and the one you want; the fifth (unused) letter tells you which equation to pick.
detail.everyday_analogy_md: Like a recipe card where any 3 ingredients tell you the other 2: if you know how many cookies, how many per tray, and how long each tray takes, you can work out the total time.
detail.visualize_md: Draw a 5-box table: s | u | v | a | t. Fill in what you know, put ? in the one you want, and a ✗ in the one you neither know nor need.

atomic_steps.step_md: Write s, u, v, a, t in a column.
Fill in the known values with signs.
Mark the unknown you want with ?.
Cross out the quantity that is neither known nor wanted.
Pick the equation without the crossed-out letter.

formulas.name: No v
formulas.when_to_use_md: When $v$ is not involved, e.g. time to fall from rest.

formulas.name: No t
formulas.when_to_use_md: When time is not involved, e.g. braking distance.

common_traps.fix_md: Check the word *constant/uniform* or that only gravity acts.
Decide the positive direction once and apply it to every vector.

tips_tricks.tip_md: The ✗ trick: the equation without the unwanted letter is always the one.

self_check: Which equation would you use if time isn't mentioned?

concepts.name: Projectile motion
concepts.one_liner: Split the flight into two independent motions: steady sideways, accelerating downwards.

detail.why_exists_md: A thrown ball moves sideways and falls at the same time: one curved path that looks hard. Splitting it into two simple straight-line motions makes it solvable with SUVAT.
detail.what_it_does_md:
Lets you find time of flight, range and impact velocity of anything thrown or launched, ignoring air resistance.

**In one sentence:** horizontal = constant speed, vertical = free fall, and the clock is shared.
detail.how_it_works_md: Gravity only pulls **down**, so it only changes vertical velocity. Horizontal velocity stays constant. Solve the vertical motion (usually to get $t$), then use that same $t$ horizontally.
detail.everyday_analogy_md: Roll a marble off a table while your friend drops one from the same height at the same moment: they hit the floor together. The sideways roll doesn't make the fall slower or faster. The floor is the "timer", and only falling matters for it.
detail.visualize_md: Imagine the shadow of the ball on the ground (moves steadily) and its shadow on a wall (falls faster and faster). The real ball is just both shadows at once.
detail.diagram_svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 320 200" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><rect x="10" y="40" width="50" height="150" fill="none" stroke="#4b5563" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M60 40 Q 170 50 250 190" fill="none" stroke="#6366f1" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/><line x1="60" y1="40" x2="110" y2="40" stroke="#4b5563" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#a)"/><defs><marker id="a" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L6,3 L0,6 z" fill="#4b5563"/></marker></defs><text x="68" y="32" fill="#4b5563">u_x (stays the same)</text><line x1="210" y1="120" x2="210" y2="160" stroke="#6366f1" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#a)"/><text x="216" y="146" fill="#6366f1">v_y grows</text><text x="16" y="120" fill="#4b5563">h</text><line x1="10" y1="190" x2="310" y2="190" stroke="#4b5563"/><text x="120" y="185" fill="#4b5563">x = u_x t</text></svg>

atomic_steps.step_md: Split velocity into horizontal $u_x$ and vertical $u_y$.

atomic_steps.everyday_link: the wall shadow falls like a dropped stone

atomic_steps.step_md: Use the same $t$ in the horizontal equation.
Recombine components with Pythagoras for speed.

formulas.name: Horizontal distance
formulas.when_to_use_md: Always, if air resistance is negligible.

common_traps.trap_md: Using the launch speed in the vertical equation.
Thinking a faster throw stays in the air longer.
common_traps.fix_md: Time depends only on vertical motion.

tips_tricks.tip_md: For horizontal launches you can skip time for impact speed: $v_y^2 = 2gh$.
Write two columns, H and V, every time.

detail.mini_example_md: Kicked horizontally at 12 m/s from 45 m: $t = \sqrt{90/9.8} = 3.03$ s; $x = 12 \times 3.03 = 36.4$ m.
self_check: Why doesn't the horizontal speed change?
What decides the time of flight?
How do you get the impact speed?

concepts.name: Newton's second law
concepts.one_liner: Resultant force = mass × acceleration: forces change motion, they don't maintain it.

detail.why_exists_md: People once thought you need a force to keep things moving. Newton showed forces **change** motion. We need a law that says exactly how much a force changes velocity.
detail.what_it_does_md:
Links the resultant (net) force on an object to its acceleration: $F = ma$.

**In one sentence:** the more unbalanced the push, and the lighter the object, the faster its velocity changes.
detail.how_it_works_md: Add all forces as vectors to get the resultant force. That resultant, and only that, causes acceleration in its direction: $a = F_{\text{net}}/m$. Balanced forces → zero acceleration (constant velocity, possibly zero).
detail.everyday_analogy_md: Pushing an empty shopping trolley vs a full one with the same push: the empty one speeds up much faster. Two friends pushing equally from opposite sides: it doesn't move (forces cancel, resultant zero).
detail.visualize_md: Draw the object as a dot with force arrows. Imagine the arrows playing tug-of-war; the leftover arrow after cancelling is $ma$.

atomic_steps.step_md: Identify every force on the object.
Add forces with signs to get the resultant.
atomic_steps.everyday_link: who wins the tug-of-war, by how much
leftover push makes it speed up

formulas.name: Newton's second law
formulas.meaning_md: Resultant force equals mass times acceleration.
formulas.when_to_use_md: Any time forces and acceleration appear together. Apply it along one direction at a time.

common_traps.trap_md: Using one force instead of the resultant.
common_traps.fix_md: Always sum *all* forces along the direction first.

common_traps.trap_md: Thinking moving objects need a forward force.
common_traps.fix_md: Constant velocity needs zero resultant force.

tips_tricks.tip_md: Resolve along the direction of acceleration and perpendicular to it.

detail.mini_example_md: A 2 kg trolley is pushed with 10 N against 4 N friction: $F_{net} = 6$ N, $a = 6/2 = 3\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.
self_check: What does a zero resultant force tell you about the motion?

concepts.name: Free-body diagrams & resolving
concepts.one_liner: Draw the object alone with every force on it, then split forces along useful directions.

detail.why_exists_md: Real situations have many things touching and pulling. A free-body diagram strips it down to *one object and the forces on it*, so you don't forget or invent forces.
detail.what_it_does_md:
Lists every force on one object and lets you resolve them into components along chosen axes.

**In one sentence:** isolate, draw arrows, choose axes, split diagonal arrows.
detail.how_it_works_md: Draw the object as a box. Add weight (down), contact forces (normal reaction perpendicular to each surface, friction along it), and tensions/pushes. On a slope choose axes along and perpendicular to the slope; resolve weight into $mg\sin\theta$ (along) and $mg\cos\theta$ (into the slope).
detail.everyday_analogy_md: Like listing who is touching you in a crowd: only people actually in contact (plus gravity pulling everyone) can push you. Nobody far away counts.
detail.visualize_md: Tilt your head to make the slope look flat: then the weight arrow is the only one that looks "slanted", so it's the only one you need to split.
detail.diagram_svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 320 200" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><defs><marker id="b" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L6,3 L0,6 z" fill="#4b5563"/></marker></defs><path d="M20 180 L300 180 L20 40 z" fill="none" stroke="#4b5563" stroke-width="2"/><g transform="rotate(26.6 140 100)"><rect x="115" y="76" width="50" height="30" fill="#eef0ff" stroke="#6366f1" stroke-width="2"/></g><line x1="140" y1="100" x2="140" y2="165" stroke="#4b5563" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#b)"/><text x="145" y="165" fill="#4b5563">mg</text><line x1="140" y1="95" x2="115" y2="45" stroke="#6366f1" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#b)"/><text x="88" y="45" fill="#6366f1">R</text><line x1="140" y1="95" x2="95" y2="73" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#b)"/><text x="60" y="80" fill="#d97706">F = μR</text><text x="255" y="172" fill="#4b5563">θ</text></svg>

atomic_steps.step_md: Draw the object alone as a box.
atomic_steps.everyday_link: cut it out of the picture

atomic_steps.step_md: Draw normal reaction perpendicular to the surface.
Draw friction along the surface, opposing sliding.
Choose axes along and perpendicular to the motion.
Resolve forces that aren't on an axis.

formulas.name: Weight component into slope
formulas.when_to_use_md: Slope problems: balances the normal reaction.

patterns_to_spot.signals_md: Axes along/perpendicular to the slope; resolve weight.
Weight, normal reaction, friction (+ any rope/push).

common_traps.fix_md: Only things touching it (plus gravity) exert forces.
As θ → 0 (flat), the along-slope part must → 0, so it's sin.

tips_tricks.tip_md: Check sin/cos with θ = 0: flat ground means no down-slope pull.

detail.mini_example_md: On a 30° slope, a 5 kg block: along $= 5 \times 9.8 \times \sin 30° = 24.5$ N; into slope $= 42.4$ N.
self_check: Which forces act on a block sliding down a rough slope?
How can you check sin vs cos quickly?

concepts.name: Friction on an inclined plane
concepts.one_liner: Friction opposes sliding with size μR, where R = mg cos θ on a slope.

detail.why_exists_md: Real slopes are rough: blocks slide slower than on ice. We need a model for how big that resistance is.
detail.what_it_does_md:
Gives the friction force $F = \mu R$ (sliding) and combines with Newton's second law to find accelerations on rough slopes.

**In one sentence:** friction = roughness × how hard the surfaces press together.
detail.how_it_works_md: The harder two surfaces press ($R$), and the rougher they are ($\mu$), the bigger the friction. On a slope, $R = mg\cos\theta$, so $F = \mu mg\cos\theta$, acting up the slope for a block sliding down. Then $ma = mg\sin\theta - \mu mg\cos\theta$.
detail.everyday_analogy_md: Sliding down a playground slide in shorts vs in rubber boots: boots = bigger μ. A heavier kid presses harder (bigger R), so more friction, but also more pull down the slope, so mass cancels!
detail.visualize_md: Picture the slide surface: friction is a hand on the block pushing back up the slide, with strength μ × (how hard the slide pushes back).

atomic_steps.everyday_link: how hard the slide pushes on you

atomic_steps.step_md: Point friction opposite to the sliding.

formulas.name: Sliding friction
formulas.when_to_use_md: When the object slides (or is about to).

formulas.name: Acceleration down a rough slope
formulas.when_to_use_md: Released block sliding down; check $\tan\theta > \mu$ for it to slide.

common_traps.trap_md: Friction pointing down the slope for a block sliding down.

tips_tricks.tip_md: Mass cancels in $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu\cos\theta)$: a quick check of your answer.

self_check: Which way does friction act on a block sliding down?

patterns.name: Horizontal launch from a height
patterns.description: Something leaves a height horizontally; find time of flight, range, impact speed, and explain independence.

source_questions.text_md:
A ball is kicked **horizontally** at $12\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ from the top of a cliff $45\ \text{m}$ high. Air resistance is negligible. Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Calculate the time the ball takes to reach the ground. **(3 marks)**

(b) Calculate the horizontal distance it travels. **(2 marks)**

(c) Calculate its speed just before it hits the ground. **(3 marks)**

(d) Explain why kicking it faster would **not** change your answer to (a). **(2 marks)**

A stone is thrown **horizontally** at $8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ from the top of a bridge $20\ \text{m}$ high. Air resistance is negligible. Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Calculate the time the stone takes to reach the ground. **(3 marks)**

(b) Calculate the horizontal distance it travels. **(2 marks)**

(c) Calculate its speed just before it hits the ground. **(3 marks)**

(d) Explain why throwing it faster would **not** change your answer to (a). **(2 marks)**

recognition_cues: a height (cliff, table, bridge) is given
asks for time, horizontal distance or impact speed

recipe.why_md: Time is set by the fall.

recipe.step_md: Sanity-check: $v$ is bigger than both components.

tricks: $v_y^2 = 2gh$ gives impact vertical speed without finding $t$.
Mass never appears: if you're using it, stop.
traps: Putting the launch speed into the vertical equation.
Forgetting to square-root at the end.
guide.examiner_wants_md: Equation quoted before substitution, $u_y = 0$ stated, units on every answer, 3 s.f. For the *explain* part: independence of components **and** time depends only on vertical quantities.

patterns.name: Block on a rough incline
patterns.description: A block on a rough slope: identify forces, find normal reaction, acceleration, then speed after a distance.

source_questions.text_md:
A block of mass $5\ \text{kg}$ is released from rest on a rough plane inclined at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal. The coefficient of friction between the block and the plane is $0.2$. Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Identify the forces acting on the block. **(2 marks)**

(b) Calculate the normal reaction force. **(2 marks)**

(c) Calculate the acceleration of the block down the plane. **(4 marks)**

(d) Calculate the speed of the block after it has slid $3\ \text{m}$. **(2 marks)**

A block of mass $2\ \text{kg}$ is released from rest on a rough plane inclined at $25^\circ$ to the horizontal. The coefficient of friction between the block and the plane is $0.15$. Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Identify the forces acting on the block. **(2 marks)**

(b) Calculate the normal reaction force. **(2 marks)**

(c) Calculate the acceleration of the block down the plane. **(4 marks)**

(d) Calculate the speed of the block after it has slid $4\ \text{m}$. **(2 marks)**

recipe.step_md: Draw the free-body diagram: $mg$, $R$, friction up the slope.
recipe.why_md: Can't sum forces you haven't drawn.
Newton's second law along the motion.

recipe.step_md: Solve for $a$, then use SUVAT for later parts.

tricks: $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu\cos\theta)$: mass cancels, a quick check.
guide.examiner_wants_md: A labelled force diagram, resolving shown in both directions, $F = \mu R$ quoted, answers to 3 s.f. with units.

patterns.name: Uniform braking / accelerating vehicle
patterns.description: A vehicle speeds up or slows uniformly: find acceleration, time or distance with SUVAT.

source_questions.text_md:
A car travelling at $25\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ brakes with uniform deceleration and comes to rest in $50\ \text{m}$.

(a) Calculate the deceleration. **(3 marks)**

(b) Calculate the time taken to stop. **(2 marks)**

recipe.step_md: List s, u, v, a, t with signs.
Cross out the one not given and not wanted.
Use the equation without that letter.

tricks: Deceleration answers carry a minus sign as $a$; state the magnitude in words.
guide.examiner_wants_md: SUVAT list shown, equation quoted, sign of acceleration interpreted.

mcqs.question_md: You jog one full lap of a 400 m track in 100 s. What is your average velocity?
option_explanations: Right: you end where you started, so displacement is 0.
That's average *speed* (distance/time), not velocity.
Units and size are off.
Mass has nothing to do with velocity.

options: Velocity can be negative; speed cannot
Speed and velocity are always equal
Displacement is always larger than distance
option_explanations: Velocity carries direction (sign); speed is its size.
Only for straight-line motion in the + direction.
Displacement is never larger than distance.
Direction is what makes it velocity.

mcqs.question_md: A ball is thrown straight up. At the very top, its velocity is zero. Its acceleration there is…
option_explanations: Gravity never switches off; it keeps changing the velocity.
Classic trap: v = 0 doesn't mean a = 0, or it would stay up there forever.
Gravity pulls down.
No.

mcqs.question_md: A bike goes from 2 m/s to 8 m/s in 3 s. Its acceleration is…
option_explanations: That's the change in velocity, not per second.
That's 10/3: you added instead of subtracting.
You multiplied.

mcqs.question_md: Which idea do you need in order to connect forces to changes in motion?
option_explanations: F = ma: force links to motion through acceleration.
Displacement alone says nothing about forces.
Distance doesn't connect to force directly.
Average speed doesn't either.

mcqs.question_md: "A car travelling at 20 m/s brakes uniformly and stops in 40 m. Find the deceleration." Which equation goes first?
option_explanations: No time is given or wanted: use the equation without $t$.
Needs $t$, which you don't have.
Needs $t$ too.
No forces or mass given.

mcqs.question_md: When can you use the SUVAT equations?
options: Only when the object starts from rest
option_explanations: They're derived assuming constant $a$.
Changing acceleration breaks them.
$u$ can be anything.
They work in any straight line.

mcqs.question_md: Two balls are dropped from rest; one falls for 2 s, the other for 4 s. The second falls…
option_explanations: $s = \tfrac12gt^2$: doubling $t$ quadruples $s$.
Distance isn't proportional to time when accelerating.
No.
That would be $t^3$.

mcqs.question_md: You roll a marble off a table and at the same instant drop another from the same height. Which lands first?
option_explanations: Vertical motion is identical (u_y = 0, same h, same g).
Sideways speed doesn't change the fall.
Same fall for both.
Mass doesn't affect free fall (no air resistance).

mcqs.question_md: During a projectile's flight (no air resistance), the horizontal velocity…
option_explanations: No horizontal force → no horizontal acceleration.
Only if air resistance acts.
Nothing pushes it sideways.
That's the vertical velocity (for an upward launch).

mcqs.question_md: "A stone is thrown horizontally from a 20 m cliff…" To find the time of flight, use…
options: The horizontal motion with the throw speed
option_explanations: Time is set by falling 20 m.
Horizontal motion doesn't set the time.
That gives impact speed, not time.
Possible for speed, not for time.

mcqs.question_md: A hockey puck slides across smooth ice at constant velocity. The resultant force on it is…
option_explanations: Constant velocity = zero acceleration = zero resultant force.
No force is needed to *keep* moving.
That would slow it down.
Weight is balanced by the normal reaction.

mcqs.question_md: A 4 kg box is pushed with 20 N against 8 N of friction. Its acceleration is…
option_explanations: 20/4: you forgot friction.
(20 + 8)/4: friction opposes, subtract it.
8/4: wrong force.

mcqs.question_md: A block slides down a rough slope. Which force does NOT act on it?
options: A "force of motion" down the slope
option_explanations: There's no such force; motion continues without a force.
Always acts.
The slope pushes back.
Rough → friction.

mcqs.question_md: On a slope of angle θ, the component of weight pulling the block DOWN the slope is $mg\sin\theta$. Quick check?
options: At θ = 0 (flat) it must be zero, and sin 0 = 0
At θ = 0 it must equal mg
At θ = 90° it must be zero
option_explanations: Flat ground doesn't pull you sideways, so the formula must vanish at 0.
On flat ground nothing pulls you along.
On a vertical wall, all of the weight is along it.
Limiting cases are the quick check.

mcqs.question_md: Block on a 30° slope, μ = 0.2. Normal reaction for a 5 kg block (g = 9.8)?
option_explanations: $5 \times 9.8 \times \cos30°$.
That's $mg$: you forgot to resolve.
That's $mg\sin30°$.
No.

mcqs.question_md: Two identical-material blocks, 1 kg and 10 kg, are released on the same rough slope. Which accelerates faster?
option_explanations: $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu\cos\theta)$: no $m$ in it.
More pull, but also more friction, in the same ratio.
Mass cancels.
If tan θ > μ they slide.

mcqs.question_md: "Released from rest on a rough plane inclined at 25°… find the acceleration." The first equation you write is…
option_explanations: You need $R$ before you can get friction $\mu R$.
That's for later parts (speed after a distance).
Not a real relation here.
Kinematics comes after you have $a$.

c-projectile-motion.question_md: You drop a ball from your hand. Which way does gravity pull it?
Now you throw the ball sideways. Does gravity pull it sideways at all?
c-projectile-motion.explanation_md: Gravity doesn't care how you threw it: still only down.

c-projectile-motion.question_md: If nothing pushes the ball sideways (no air resistance), what happens to its sideways speed?
c-projectile-motion.explanation_md: No sideways force → no sideways acceleration → constant sideways speed.

c-projectile-motion.question_md: So does throwing it sideways change how fast it falls?
options: No: falling is a separate motion
c-projectile-motion.explanation_md: **This is projectile motion:** two independent motions, sideways at constant speed and downwards like a dropped ball, sharing one clock.

c-newtons-second-law.question_md: Same push on an empty trolley and a full one. Which speeds up faster?
c-newtons-second-law.explanation_md: Less mass → bigger change of speed for the same push.

c-newtons-second-law.question_md: Two friends push one trolley equally hard from opposite sides. What happens?
c-newtons-second-law.explanation_md: The pushes cancel: the **resultant** force is zero.

options: The leftover (resultant) force and the mass
c-newtons-second-law.explanation_md: **Newton's second law:** $F_{net} = ma$. Resultant force, divided by mass, gives acceleration.

problems.title: Ball kicked from a cliff
problems.statement_md:
A ball is kicked **horizontally** at $12\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ from the top of a cliff $45\ \text{m}$ high. Air resistance is negligible. Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Calculate the time the ball takes to reach the ground. **(3 marks)**

(b) Calculate the horizontal distance it travels. **(2 marks)**

(c) Calculate its speed just before it hits the ground. **(3 marks)**

(d) Explain why kicking it faster would **not** change your answer to (a). **(2 marks)**

steps.prompt_md: Which of these does the question give you (directly or by its wording)? Select all.
steps.hint_md: "Horizontally" is information too: what does it say about the starting vertical velocity?
steps.explanation_md: Given: $u_x=12$, $h=45$, $g=9.8$. The word *horizontally* tells you $u_y = 0$. Mass and time are **not** given (and mass is never needed).

steps.prompt_md: Which motion decides how long the object is in the air?
steps.hint_md: What has to happen for the flight to end? It has to *fall* 45 m... or whatever the height is.
steps.explanation_md: The flight ends when the object has fallen the full height. Falling is vertical motion, controlled only by $u_y$, $g$ and $h$.

steps.prompt_md: Which SUVAT equation links $s$, $u$, $a$ and $t$ (no $v$)?
steps.hint_md: You know $s$, $u$, $a$ and want $t$. You don't know the final vertical velocity $v$.

steps.prompt_md: With $u_y = 0$, rearrange $h = \tfrac12 g t^2$ for $t$.
steps.hint_md: Multiply both sides by 2, divide by $g$, then undo the square.

steps.prompt_md: Compute $2h/g$ (the value under the square root).
So what is the time of flight $t$?
What is the horizontal acceleration during the flight?
steps.explanation_md: Gravity is vertical. Horizontally nothing pushes or pulls, so $u_x$ stays constant.

steps.prompt_md: Which formula gives the horizontal distance?
Calculate the horizontal distance $x$.
Find the vertical velocity $v_y$ just before impact.
How do you combine the two velocity components into a speed?
steps.hint_md: The components are at right angles, like the two short sides of a right triangle.

steps.prompt_md: Calculate the impact speed $v$.
Sanity check: the impact speed must be…
steps.hint_md: The hypotenuse of a right triangle vs its two sides.
steps.explanation_md: A hypotenuse is longer than either side but shorter than their sum.

parts.label: d
parts.final_answer_md: Vertical and horizontal motion are independent; time depends only on $h$ and $g$.

steps.prompt_md: Explain why launching faster does not change the time of flight.
steps.text_answer_md:
- Horizontal and vertical motions are **independent** (perpendicular). (1)
- The time is set by the vertical motion only: $u_y = 0$, $h$ and $g$ are unchanged, so $t = \sqrt{2h/g}$ is unchanged. (1)
steps.explanation_md: Marks go for (1) independence of components and (2) time depends only on vertical quantities, which are unchanged.

problems.title: Block on a rough 30° slope
problems.statement_md:
A block of mass $5\ \text{kg}$ is released from rest on a rough plane inclined at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal. The coefficient of friction between the block and the plane is $0.2$. Take $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Identify the forces acting on the block. **(2 marks)**

(b) Calculate the normal reaction force. **(2 marks)**

(c) Calculate the acceleration of the block down the plane. **(4 marks)**

(d) Calculate the speed of the block after it has slid $3\ \text{m}$. **(2 marks)**

parts.label: a
parts.final_answer_md: Weight (down), normal reaction (perpendicular to the plane), friction (up the slope).

steps.prompt_md: What does the question give you? Select all.
choices: A pushing force on the block
steps.explanation_md: Rough = friction acts. Released from rest = $u = 0$. Nothing pushes it.

steps.prompt_md: Which forces act on the block as it slides down? Select all.
choices: Normal reaction, perpendicular to the plane
"The force of motion" down the slope
steps.hint_md: Friction always opposes the sliding. Is there anything *touching* the block besides the plane?
steps.explanation_md: Only three forces: weight, normal reaction, and friction opposing motion (so up the slope). "Force of motion" doesn't exist: motion needs no force to continue.

steps.prompt_md: Resolving perpendicular to the plane, the normal reaction is…
steps.hint_md: No acceleration perpendicular to the plane, so forces balance in that direction. Which component of weight points into the plane?

steps.prompt_md: Calculate $R$.
Component of the weight acting down the slope, $mg\sin\theta$:
Friction force $F = \mu R$:
Newton's second law along the slope (down = positive):
steps.hint_md: Resultant force = (force pulling down the slope) − (force resisting).
steps.explanation_md: Resultant force down the slope is $mg\sin\theta - F$, and it equals $ma$.

steps.prompt_md: Calculate the acceleration $a$.
Which equation links $u$, $v$, $a$ and $s$ (no $t$)?
Calculate $v$.

problems.title: Car braking to rest
problems.statement_md:
A car travelling at $25\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ brakes with uniform deceleration and comes to rest in $50\ \text{m}$.

(a) Calculate the deceleration. **(3 marks)**

(b) Calculate the time taken to stop. **(2 marks)**

steps.prompt_md: Match the question to SUVAT. Which values are known? Select all.
steps.hint_md: "Comes to rest" gives you one of them.
steps.explanation_md: $u$, $v=0$ (rest) and $s$ are known; $a$ and $t$ are not.

steps.prompt_md: Which equation uses $u$, $v$, $s$ and $a$ only?
Calculate $a$ (include the sign).
steps.explanation_md: $a = -625/(2 \times 50) = -6.25\ \text{m s}^{-2}$; negative because it slows down.

steps.prompt_md: Quickest equation for $t$ now?
Calculate $t$.

problems.title: Train braking to rest
problems.statement_md:
A car travelling at $30\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ brakes with uniform deceleration and comes to rest in $225\ \text{m}$.

(a) Calculate the deceleration. **(3 marks)**

(b) Calculate the time taken to stop. **(2 marks)**

steps.prompt_md: Match the question to SUVAT. Which values are known? Select all.
steps.hint_md: "Comes to rest" gives you one of them.
steps.explanation_md: $u$, $v=0$ (rest) and $s$ are known; $a$ and $t$ are not.

steps.prompt_md: Which equation uses $u$, $v$, $s$ and $a$ only?
Calculate $a$ (include the sign).
steps.explanation_md: $a = -900/(2 \times 225) = -2.00\ \text{m s}^{-2}$; negative because it slows down.

Calculate $t$.
